title: Manual do Mundo
author: Iberê Thenório
review: I was seven and the book smelled like fresh paint. Every experiment had this confident tone that made science feel like something you did at the kitchen table, not something you watched adults do on TV. The chapter on homemade rockets kept me up until midnight building one out of a plastic bottle. Rating feels obvious but it earned it: this is the book that made me a person who asks 'what happens if I mix these.'

title: How to Train Your Dragon
author: Cressida Cowell
review: Hiccup is small, bad at everything the tribe values, and wins anyway by being smarter than the problem requires. At nine I didn't have words for 'unconventional competitive advantage' but the book planted the idea. The humor is dry in a way I didn't fully get until rereading it years later. Not transcendent, but I kept thinking about Hiccup's method of persuasion long after I forgot the plot.

title: Percy Jackson
subtitle: The Lightning Thief
author: Rick Riordan
review: I read the whole series in two months. The trick Riordan pulls is that he makes Greek mythology feel like background knowledge you already have, so you never feel like you're being taught. Annabeth is better written than Percy and I don't think that's an accident. The ending of the first book has a betrayal that I genuinely did not see coming at ten, which is harder to achieve than it sounds.

title: A Ilha do Tesouro
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
review: Long John Silver is the most interesting character because the book can't quite decide if he's the villain. He saves Jim twice. He switches sides when it suits him and you almost respect him for it. Stevenson wrote adventure fiction and accidentally wrote a study in moral ambiguity. I read it in Portuguese and some of the nautical vocabulary I had to ask about, which made me feel like I was actually on the ship.

title: Harry Potter
subtitle: Complete Series
author: J.K. Rowling
review: The series that turned reading into a compulsion. Books five and six did something most fantasy series refuse to do: made the world worse as the protagonist gets more powerful, which felt honest. I cried at the end of book seven, which I was mildly embarrassed about at eleven. I've since stopped being embarrassed. The lore doesn't hold up to hard scrutiny and I don't care, because the emotional scaffolding is solid.

title: O Pijama Listrado
author: John Boyne
review: The ending arrived faster than I expected and I sat with the book closed for a few minutes after. Boyne makes the horror visible by routing it through a child's incomplete understanding, which is a technique that shouldn't work as well as it does. I read it in one sitting on a Sunday afternoon, which I remember specifically because I went quiet at dinner and my parents asked what was wrong.

title: Auto da Compadecida
author: Ariano Suassuna
review: João Grilo wins every fight by being the smartest person in the room and also the most willing to humiliate himself. Suassuna builds a whole theology out of Northeastern Brazilian folk culture and it's completely coherent. The trial scene in the third act is the funniest thing I read before age fifteen. It's also deeply sad if you think about what João Grilo actually wants versus what he gets. Brazilian literature has nothing else quite like this.

title: O Extraordinário
author: R.J. Palacio
review: Multiple perspectives on the same events, and each one notices different things. What I remember most is Jack's chapter, where he doesn't realize he's being cruel until after. The book made me think about how many times I've been Jack without noticing. Palacio doesn't let anyone be cleanly good or bad, and for a middle-grade novel that's more than you'd expect. Changed something small in how I treat people.

title: Dom Casmurro
author: Machado de Assis
review: I'm still not sure Capitu did it, and I think that's on purpose. Bentinho is an unreliable narrator who doesn't know he's unreliable, which Machado executes without once winking at the reader. The prose is technically impressive. I gave it a four because the jealousy spiral gets repetitive around the midpoint, and I found myself skimming to find out if the evidence ever becomes real evidence. It doesn't. That's the point. I know.

title: Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
review: The narrator opens by noting he died. He spends the rest of the book being wrong about himself in very specific ways. Machado is doing something formally strange for 1881 and the book reads almost contemporary because of it. Four stars because Brás Cubas is deliberately insufferable, which is the author's point but still makes some chapters slow to get through. The chapter called 'O delírio' is worth the whole book alone.

title: Física - Renato Brito Vol. 1
author: Renato Brito
review: The mechanics chapter changed how I think about forces: not as things that push objects, but as constraints on motion. Renato Brito writes textbook problems that have a logic to them, so solving them feels less like grinding and more like following an argument. I worked through every exercise in this volume. It's the reason I started doing well in physics olympiads. A textbook that teaches you to think before it teaches you to calculate.

title: Física - Renato Brito Vol. 2
author: Renato Brito
review: Electromagnetism is where physics gets abstract and a lot of people lose the thread. This volume builds the intuition slowly and I didn't feel lost the way I did with other references. The thermodynamics section is denser and I had to reread some of it, which I count as a feature. By the end I could look at a circuit diagram and see the energy flows rather than just the connections. That shift in perception took a few months of working through this book.

title: Tópicos de Física
author: Gualter, Helou & Nicolau
review: The standard Brazilian physics textbook and it shows: solid explanations, good problem sets, nothing surprising. I used it mostly as a reference to cross-check things I'd learned from Renato Brito, and for that purpose it worked well. The optical diagrams are cleaner than most alternatives. Four stars because it gets the job done without any particular elegance. If you're studying for vestibular, it has everything. If you want to enjoy physics, start elsewhere.

title: Duna
author: Frank Herbert
review: The ecology of Arrakis is more thought-out than most real political science. Herbert stacks ecology, religion, colonial economics, and messianic psychology into one story and doesn't simplify any of them. I read it in Portuguese at fourteen and had to stop several times to look up what the Fremen were actually saying to each other below the surface conversation. The ending refuses to be a happy ending. That bothered me at first and then I understood why it was the only honest choice.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
quote: Nothing is so painful to the human mind as a great and sudden change.
review: Not the monster story I expected. Victor Frankenstein is the actual problem in this book and Shelley makes that clear early. The creature's speech in the middle section is more articulate and self-aware than anything Victor manages. My one complaint is that the frame structure with Walton slows the opening significantly. The question the book keeps asking is what you owe something you brought into existence knowing it would suffer. I didn't have a clean answer at fifteen. I still don't.

title: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
quote: A book is a loaded gun in the house next door.
review: Short and dense and genuinely unsettling. Bradbury's version of censorship is scarier than Orwell's because it doesn't require a dictator: people just stop reading voluntarily, and the firemen are almost redundant by the time the story happens. Mildred's storyline is the part that stuck with me, not Montag's. The ending works as both hope and a warning, which is harder to write than it looks. I read this in one afternoon and felt like I'd had a conversation I needed to have.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
review: More unsettling than 1984 because the mechanism of control is comfort, not pain. Nobody's being tortured; they're just satisfied enough that resistance feels pointless. The Savage's argument with Mustapha Mond near the end is the actual thesis of the book and it's one of the most honestly written dialogues I've read: Mond doesn't lie, he just explains why the tradeoff is worth it, and the reader has to decide if he's wrong. I wasn't sure he was entirely wrong, which bothered me.

title: Atkins Physical Chemistry
author: Peter Atkins
review: University-level physical chemistry at sixteen because my research required the thermodynamic background. The quantum mechanics chapters are where I spent most of my time, and Atkins explains molecular orbital theory clearly enough that the math stops feeling abstract. Some sections, especially electrochemistry, assume lab context I didn't have, which made them harder to connect. Four stars because it's written as a companion to a course, and I was reading it alone. As a reference it's excellent. As a self-study text, parts of it require patience.

title: The Martian
author: Andy Weir
review: Watney's voice is almost aggressively cheerful for someone who might die of botany failure, and that gap between tone and stakes is where the book lives. The science is mostly correct and Weir doesn't hide the math, which means you can follow the logic of every improvised solution. The part where NASA runs orbital mechanics on a whiteboard and then realizes they forgot to carry a number is the funniest scene in hard sci-fi I've read. Engineering as a survival strategy landed differently after I started building products.

title: Project Hail Mary
author: Andy Weir
review: Better than The Martian. The science problem is more elegant, the stakes are higher, and then Weir introduces Rocky and the book becomes something else entirely. Building a shared language from first principles to solve a problem together, with nothing in common except curiosity and necessity, is a premise I'd read a hundred times. The ending is the correct ending. It will make you feel something specific that I won't describe. Rocky is the best fictional character in either of Weir's books.

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
author: Richard Feynman
review: Not really a physics book. It's a book about how to be curious without caring what that looks like. Feynman is sometimes insufferable and I think he knows it and includes it anyway, which is more honest than most memoirs. The safecracking chapters are funny in a way that requires no physics background. The chapter where he describes learning to draw because he wanted to give something to people who couldn't follow the equations stuck with me. The best scientists are also translators.

title: The Complete Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
review: Over a thousand pages and the quality stays consistent because Holmes is a method, not just a character. The short stories work better than the novels because the deduction chains are tighter. Watson is the real narrative achievement: he makes Holmes readable by being the person who finds Holmes impressive instead of exhausting. I read the whole thing across several months and it trained something in how I look at problems, specifically the habit of generating multiple hypotheses before committing to any explanation.

title: The Official SAT Study Guide
author: College Board
review: Nobody reads this for pleasure. You read it to understand the test well enough that the test stops being a test and starts being a pattern you recognize. I worked through eight full practice tests with timed sections. The math is easier than Brazilian olympiad math but the time pressure is harder. The reading comprehension questions have a specific logic once you understand that every correct answer must be supported by exact text, which sounds obvious and isn't. The discipline it required was more useful than any individual skill it taught.

title: The Wolf of Wall Street
author: Jordan Belfort
review: Belfort writes his own disaster with too much energy for it to function as a cautionary tale, and I think he knows it. The selling techniques buried in the chaos are actually sound. What the book demonstrates, unintentionally, is that exceptional sales ability in an unethical system doesn't produce exceptional outcomes: it produces exceptional destruction at scale. The parts where he describes losing control of the organization he built are more interesting than the parts about getting rich. A useful read if you're building something, mostly for the negative examples.

title: Catching the Wolf of Wall Street
author: Jordan Belfort
review: Better written than the first book in some ways because Belfort can't glamorize what's happening. The cooperation process is fascinating in a procedural sense: who flips first, what the FBI actually needs, how long you can hold a front together under investigation. The moments where Belfort starts genuinely respecting the agents pursuing him are the most honest parts of the book. Four stars because the pacing drags in the middle third and some of the legal detail stops being interesting. Worth reading after the first one.

title: The Way of the Wolf
author: Jordan Belfort
review: The straight-line system is less about manipulation and more about reducing uncertainty for both sides of a conversation. The core idea is that objections are usually not about the stated objection. Once you accept that, the whole framework follows logically. I use pieces of this when pitching HIBEEX: not the scripts, but the underlying model of what someone needs to believe before they say yes. Shorter and more applicable than I expected from a sales book written by someone with Belfort's reputation.

title: Made in America
author: Sam Walton
review: Walton's competitive obsession is constant but it never tips into arrogance because he spends most of the book describing what he got wrong and who he learned from. The store visits chapter, where he flew his own plane between locations to check prices and talk to floor staff, is a better operations manual than most business books I've read. The humility reads as real rather than performed because he keeps giving credit for specific decisions to specific people. Still reading, currently at the chapter on distribution.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
review: The monopoly argument is the useful part and Thiel states it plainly: competition destroys the margin that funds innovation, so the goal is to build something nobody else is building. The chapter on secrets is the one I think about most. His definition of a secret is something that is true, that most people don't believe, and that you can act on. Building HIBEEX required having a specific answer to that question. The contrarian framing is sometimes overextended but the core thesis earns it.
